about: Ten real home-service negotiations from one homeowner's own history (2026), paraphrased in our own words. Names, companies, places, phone numbers and dates are removed; money is given only as ratios to the first quote. Each case seeds one buyer archetype in the tournament. Source notes are private and not in this repository.

cases.story: After a small repair quote the customer named a ceiling of about 70% of it and said otherwise they would skip the job. The shop agreed within minutes and won the job. The work later turned into a dispute.
cases.lesson: A fast concession inside the customer's stated ceiling wins; speed matters. Conceding is not free of risk.

cases.story: The customer had a competing all-in quote at roughly 55% of this one and offered to book at about 80% for a specific day. The shop agreed to 80% only after two and a half days; by then the customer had hired the competitor, who replied three times within hours and offered next-day service.
cases.lesson: The same concession lost because it came too late. Speed of the concession decides.

cases.story: The shop cut its price twice within ninety minutes, to roughly a quarter of the first quote, and still lost: the customer had a do-it-yourself plan.
cases.lesson: When the customer's real alternative is far below any sane floor, deeper discounts do not win. Holding the floor is right.

cases.story: Without being asked, the shop knocked about 11% off in a 'final follow-up' message, and the customer booked.
cases.lesson: The job was won, but the customer had not asked for a discount: some of that money was given away.

cases.story: After the customer said the diagnostic price was high, the shop made a good counter-offer (about half price, or a payment plan). The customer did not see it for ten days because it went to a channel they did not check, and the job was lost for that reason, not on price.
cases.lesson: An offer on the wrong channel does not exist. Resend where the customer reads.

cases.story: The customer asked for a smaller scope at a much lower price; the shop held its price and said it was booked all week. The add-on work was lost because of the schedule, not the price.
cases.lesson: When the customer needs it sooner, an earlier slot is the move; a discount does not help.

cases.story: A large whole-house quote was followed by seven text messages, calls and emails over seven weeks, none with a new offer. The customer had said they would do part of the work themselves; a labour-only option at about a fifth of the quote was never offered.
cases.lesson: Reminders without a new offer do not work. Offer a smaller package when the customer signals scope.

cases.story: Three weeks after the quote the shop sent '15% off for everyone who got an estimate'. It did not work: the decision was waiting on another family member.
cases.lesson: A discount does not move a decision that is waiting on someone else.

cases.story: At home the family decided one part of the job was too expensive and never told the shop. Three weeks later the shop wrote 'you have gone quiet'. There was an objection; the shop only saw silence.
cases.lesson: Silence can hide a specific line-item objection. Ask, and offer the job without that item.

cases.story: A losing electrician asked how his price compared; the winner had charged less than half. Quotes for the same scope ranged about five-fold.
cases.lesson: Some price objections cannot be won inside the owner's floor; the agent should not chase them below it.

aggregate: Across about 45 priced quotes, about 18 went quiet or got a 'not yet'. About 20 shops followed up after silence; 3-4 recovered the job. Price was a minority of the reasons; pauses, family decisions and missed messages were more common.
